newsitem.title: GREECE: ATHLETICS-BOLDON LOOKS SET TO INHERIT BAILEY'S SPRINT CROWN.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-BOLDON LOOKS SET TO INHERIT BAILEY'S SPRINT CROWN.

text.p: Ato Boldon equalled the fourth fastest 100 metres time in history on Saturday when he clocked a year's best of 9.87 seconds on the opening day of the world championships.
The time, aided by a following wind of 1.3 metres a second, was also a personal best and underlined Boldon's claim for the world title on Sunday.
"If you have a lightning fast track, the hot weather and the wind blowing in the right direction, you'll get the year's fastest race," said a delighted Boldon..
"That's why I'm telling you, you will probably see a world record tomorrow in the final. My dream is to run the 100 in 9.80 seconds but I'll be happy with 9.81.
"I don't want to insult the record, but it's soft and should be lower."

Boldon, the Olympic bronze medallist last year who has repeatedly predicted that Donovan Bailey's world record time of 9.84 seconds would fall on Sunday, looks like being proved right as most of the winning times were quick.
Namibian Frankie Fredericks, second in the Atlanta Olympic final, clocked 9.99 seconds as did American Tim Montgomery who came home ahead of Bailey (10.10) in his heat in ideal conditions.
Boldon blazed out of the blocks, and ran with superbly controlled aggression to head home American champion Maurice Greene who was second in 9.90 seconds.
Boldon even looked across at his training partner as they flashed across the line.
"It is going to be a wonderful final," said Greene. "The record is gone."

Only Bailey (9.84), American Leroy Burrell (9.85), Carl Lewis and Frankie Fredericks (both 9.86) have ever run a legal faster time. Linford Christie of Britain also clocked 9.87 seconds when he won the world title in Stuttgart in 1993.
Bailey, meanwhile, appeared to be wincing and in some pain as he crossed the line behind Montgomery in his heat.
He hobbled through the mixed zone after the race, threw his shoe basket down in disgust and unusually refused to discuss the race with the media before leaving with his manager Ray Flynn.
Asked if Bailey was suffering from cramp, Flynn said: "It certainly looked like that, but I am not sure."

Montgomery said: "Boldon and Greene have proved a point which is if you can run that relaxed and that fast through the rounds you are sending a very strong message which can shake up the other runners."

As in the opening round in the morning, Bailey had a poor start but accelerated through the field in the second half of the race. But he was visibly in trouble over the last seven or eight metres and was grimacing as he crossed the line.
Former Olympic 200 metres champion Mike Marsh advanced with a time of 10.05 while Canadian Bruny Surin also reached Sunday's semifinal with 10.06.
